**Given:** $0<w<1$, $\epsilon>0$, $\epsilon_*>0$, $N_*>0$, and the EOS-defined functions of [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]] and [[lem-emg-charged-fluid-positive-symmetric-reduction]].

[F1] [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]]: $N(\epsilon)=N_*\exp(\int_{\epsilon_*}^{\epsilon}(z+p(z))^{-1}\,dz)$, with $N_*>0$.

[F2] [[lem-emg-charged-fluid-positive-symmetric-reduction]]: $r(\epsilon)=\int_{\epsilon_*}^{\epsilon}\sqrt{p'(z)}/(z+p(z))\,dz$ and $r'=\sqrt{p'}/(\epsilon+p)>0$ for the strict EOS.



**Proof technique:** direct integral evaluation and differentiation.

1.1 The derivative of $p(\epsilon)=w\epsilon$ is $p'=w$. Since $w>0$ and $\epsilon>0$, $p'=w\in(0,1)$ and $\epsilon+p=(1+w)\epsilon>0$ on $J$. Thus the strict EOS hypotheses hold. [given, algebra]

1.2 For every $z>0$, $(z+p(z))^{-1}=((1+w)z)^{-1}$. Substituting this in [F1] and integrating gives $N=N_*\exp((1+w)^{-1}\log(\epsilon/\epsilon_*))=N_*(\epsilon/\epsilon_*)^{1/(1+w)}$. The logarithm is dimensionless because both arguments are energy densities. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $\sqrt{p'(z)}=\sqrt w$, [F2] gives $r=(\sqrt w/(1+w))\log(\epsilon/\epsilon_*)$. Differentiating yields $r'=\sqrt w/((1+w)\epsilon)>0$, so $r$ is strictly increasing. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ its logarithm tends to $-\infty$, and as $\epsilon\to\infty$ it tends to $+\infty$; the positive prefactor preserves these limits, so its range is all of $\mathbb R$. Solving the displayed formula gives $\epsilon/\epsilon_*=\exp((1+w)r/\sqrt w)$; inserting this in step 1.2 yields $N=N_*e^{r/\sqrt w}$. [F2, given, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The stated fields on $\mathbb R^3\times I$, with $\chi,E_0,\epsilon_i>0$ and $U=(c,0,0,0)$.

[F1] [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]: $T_m^{ab}=(\epsilon+p)U^aU^b/c^2+pg^{ab}$, $E_U^a=F^a{}_bU^b$, and the formal exchange force is $f^b=F^b{}_cj^c$.

[F2] [[thm-emg-charged-fluid-projections]]: if $q\cdot U=0$ and $q=\chi E_U$, then the comoving exchange term is $-U_bf^b=\chi g(E_U,E_U)$.

[A1] The current is imposed as $j=q$ with $q^aU_a=0$; the fixed $F$ is not asserted to satisfy the sourced Maxwell equation.



1.1 The chosen $q$ is orthogonal to $U$, and $E_U^1=F^1{}_0U^0=(E_0/c)c=E_0$, with its other components zero. Thus $q=\chi E_U$. The stress tensor has $T_m^{00}=\epsilon(t)$, $T_m^{ii}=p_0$, and zero off-diagonal components, so $\nabla_aT_m^{a0}=\partial_0\epsilon=(1/c)d\epsilon/dt=\chi E_0^2/c$ while $\nabla_aT_m^{ai}=0$. [F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 Raising the first index with $\eta$ gives $F^0{}_1=E_0/c$ and $F^i{}_1=0$ for $i=1,2,3$. Hence $f^0=F^0{}_1q^1=\chi E_0^2/c$ and $f^i=0$. The component equations verify $\nabla_aT_m^{ab}=f^b$, and [F2] gives $-U_bf^b=\chi E_0^2>0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $F$ is constant, $\nabla_aF^{ab}=0$, whereas $-\mu_0j^1=-\mu_0\chi E_0\ne0$. Thus the matter exchange and positive heating calculation is conditional on the imposed background and is not a sourced Maxwell solution. [F1, A1, algebra] ∎



The calculation is local and includes no equation of state, entropy balance, electromagnetic backreaction, or global fluid solution. The units $[\chi]=\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}$ and $[E_0]=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ make $\chi E_0^2$ a power density, but the example reports no measurement.

**Given:** Countable Choice, the EOS and current of [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]], a Lorentzian metric with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and a future unit velocity $u$.

[F1] [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]]: $\epsilon\in J$, $\epsilon+p>0$, $0<p'<1$, $g(u,u)=-1$, $j^a=cNZu^a$, and $\nabla^aT_{m,ab}=F_{bc}j^c$.

[F2] [[def-gr-barotropic-enthalpy-variable]]: Under Countable Choice, $r(\epsilon)=\int_{\epsilon_*}^{\epsilon}\sqrt{p'(z)}/(z+p(z))\,dz$ is a smooth increasing coordinate on $J$ with $r'=c_s/(\epsilon+p)>0$, and the unforced barotropic equations in $(r,u)$ are equivalent to the enthalpy equations.

[F3] [[lem-gr-barotropic-fluid-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]: For $0<c_s<1$ and a future unit velocity, the uncharged $(r,u)$ block has symmetric principal bilinear form $\zeta(u)(aa'+g(v,v'))+c_s(a\zeta(v')+a'\zeta(v))$ on $u^\perp$ variations; for future-positive timelike $\zeta$, it is positive definite.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The change of variable and derivative formula in [F2] give $\nabla_a r=c_s\nabla_a\epsilon/(\epsilon+p)$. Contracting the matter balance of [F1] with $u^b$ eliminates $u^bF_{bc}j^c$ by antisymmetry and gives $u\epsilon+(\epsilon+p)\nabla_a u^a=0$. Orthogonally projecting the same balance gives $(\epsilon+p)u^a\nabla_a u_b+(\delta_b{}^a+u_bu^a)\nabla_a p=F_{bc}j^c$. Since $\nabla_a p=p'\nabla_a\epsilon=(\epsilon+p)c_s\nabla_a r$, division by $\epsilon+p>0$ yields the displayed charged enthalpy equations reversibly; the $Z$ equation is unchanged. The extra force is algebraic, so this has the same principal $(r,u)$ equations as the uncharged system in [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Choose smooth local coordinates $y^A$ on the future unit-velocity hyperboloid and write $e_A=\partial u/\partial y^A$. Differentiating $g(u,u)=-1$ with the metric fixed gives $g(u,e_A)=0$, so $(e_A)$ spans $u^\perp$. By [F3], the four $(r,y^A)$ principal matrices are symmetric with covector contraction equal to its stated bilinear form. The independent equation $u^\mu\partial_\mu Z=0$ adds $A^\mu_{ZZ}=u^\mu$ and zero cross entries; hence the combined matrices remain symmetric. In the coupled metric reduction, metric derivatives in the connection and in the local velocity coordinates are lower-order state terms once the first metric derivatives are included as state variables. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For a future-positive timelike covector $\zeta$, the $(r,u)$ block in [F3] is positive definite. Its orthogonal direct sum with the $Z$ block has quadratic form $Q_\zeta((a,v,z),(a,v,z))=Q^{(r,u)}_\zeta((a,v),(a,v))+\zeta(u)z^2$, with $\zeta(u)>0$. It is therefore positive definite. This proves the symmetric reduction and positivity; the Lorentz force remains a lower-order source. [step 1.2, F3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Nonzero finite $H$ with the linear-first convention and the ordinary operator norm and finite trace.

[F1] [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] supplies finite Hermitian spectral calculus, positive square roots, and cyclic basis-independent trace.

[F2] [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] and [[cor-operator-norm-submultiplicative-and-t-star-t-identity]] give the induced norm, submultiplicativity and C*-identity. [[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]] gives completeness for a normed space with an ordered finite basis.

[F3] [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]], [[def-matrix-units]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]] supply an orthonormal coordinate basis, its matrix units, and vector Cauchy–Schwarz.

[F4] [[def-c-star-algebra]] specifies all C*-algebra axioms. [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] defines a state by positivity and bounded-functional norm one; only these defining clauses are used, not its general approximate-unit norm theorem. [[def-qc-density-operator]] defines a finite density by positivity and trace one.



1.1 Choose an ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_D$. Its matrix units form an ordered basis of the complex endomorphism space, since $A=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}E_{ij}$ uniquely. The operator norm is a norm: its triangle inequality and homogeneity follow by applying the vector norm to $Av$ for unit $v$, and norm zero implies $Ae_j=0$ for all $j$. Matrix composition is associative and complex bilinear, and conjugate transpose is conjugate-linear, involutive and reverses products. By [F2] the norm is submultiplicative, complete, and satisfies $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$. Thus all axioms of [F4] hold. The identity is nonzero and has norm one because $D\ge1$. The C*-identity and submultiplicativity give $\|A\|^2\le\|A^*\|\|A\|$, and applying this also to $A^*$ gives $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$, including $A=0$. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 For every vector $v$, $\langle(\|A\|^2I-A^*A)v,v\rangle=\|A\|^2\|v\|^2-\|Av\|^2\ge0$. This Hermitian matrix is positive semidefinite, so [F1] gives its positive square root. The same spectral calculus shows that matrix positivity is equivalent to being $B^*B$, agreeing with the algebraic positivity used in [F4]. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\omega$ be complex linear and positive, and define $\rho_{ij}:=\omega(E_{ji})$. Finite expansion gives $\omega(A)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\omega(E_{ij})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$. For a column vector $z$, take $B=e_1z^*$; then $B^*B=zz^*$, so $z^*\rho z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho zz^*)=\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ is real. Substitution of $z=e_i$, $e_i+e_j$, and $e_i+i e_j$ shows that the diagonal is real and $\rho_{ji}=\overline{\rho_{ij}}$; hence $\rho$ is Hermitian and its nonnegative quadratic forms make it positive semidefinite. Taking $A=I$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=\omega(I)$. The formula on the matrix units forces every entry of any representing matrix, proving uniqueness. [given, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Conversely let $\rho\ge0$ and diagonalize it by [F1] as $\rho=\sum_j p_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, $p_j\ge0$. Then $\omega_\rho(A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ is complex linear and $\omega_\rho(B^*B)=\sum_jp_j\|Bu_j\|^2\ge0$. For every complex $A$, vector Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\omega_\rho(A)|\le\sum_jp_j\|Au_j\|\le(\sum_jp_j)\|A\|$. Thus its functional norm is at most $\operatorname{Tr}\rho$, and evaluating at the norm-one identity gives the reverse inequality. This proves the norm formula, including $\rho=0$. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 give the full bijection; imposing norm one is exactly imposing trace one by [F4], with no faithfulness requirement. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** An integer $d\ge1$ and a Hermitian matrix $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$;
for the positivity conclusion, also assume $x^*Ax\ge0$ for every $x$.

[F1] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, is compact.

[F2] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real function on a nonempty
compact metric space attains its maximum.

[F3] [[thm-of-square-roots]]: every nonnegative real number has a unique
nonnegative square root.

**Proof technique:** Rayleigh maximization and induction on $d$.



1.1 Identify $\mathbb C^d$ with $\mathbb R^{2d}$ by real and imaginary coordinates. Its unit sphere is a closed bounded subset and is nonempty because $d\ge1$; it is compact by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The Rayleigh function $f(x)=x^*Ax$ is real on the unit sphere, since $A=A^*$, and is continuous because each coordinate of $f$ is a finite polynomial in the real and imaginary coordinates of $x$. By [F2] it has a maximizer $u$ with $u^*u=1$. [given, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix $w$ with $u^*w=0$ and let $g(t)=(u+tw)^*A(u+tw)/(u+tw)^*(u+tw)$ for real $t$. The denominator is $1+t^2w^*w>0$, so $g$ is differentiable near $0$; maximality of $u$ gives $g'(0)=0$. Expanding numerator and denominator gives $g'(0)=2\operatorname{Re}(w^*Au)$, hence the real part of $w^*Au$ is zero. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply step 3.1 with $iw$ in place of $w$. Since $(iw)^*Au=-i\,w^*Au$, its real part is the imaginary part of $w^*Au$; therefore $w^*Au=0$ for every $w\perp u$. Decompose $Au=(u^*Au)u+w_0$ with $w_0\perp u$; taking $w=w_0$ yields $w_0^*Au=\|w_0\|^2=0$. Thus $Au=\lambda u$, where $\lambda=u^*Au\in\mathbb R$. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $x\perp u$, then $u^*Ax=(Au)^*x=\lambda u^*x=0$, so $u^\perp$ is invariant under $A$ and the restriction of $A$ to it is Hermitian. For $d=1$ the standard unit vector is already an eigenbasis. For $d>1$, induction on the dimension supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis on $u^\perp$; adjoining $u$ gives one for $\mathbb C^d$. [step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For any unit eigenvector $v$ with eigenvalue $\mu$, positivity gives $\mu=v^*Av\ge0$. By [F3], each such $\mu$ has a unique nonnegative square root. In the eigenbasis from step 5.1, define $A^{1/2}$ to be diagonal with entries $\sqrt{\mu}$. This matrix is nonnegative and squares to $A$; it is independent of choices inside repeated eigenspaces because the same scalar is assigned to every vector in that eigenspace. [given, F3, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A complex inner-product space $H$ of finite dimension $D\geq1$, a Hermitian $M$, and an ordered orthonormal basis, whose coordinates identify $H$ isometrically with $\mathbb R^{2D}$.

[F1] [[cor-bolzano-weierstrass-in-rn]]: every bounded sequence in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq1$, has a convergent subsequence.

[F2] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the inner product is linear in the first argument, conjugate-linear in the second, and positive definite.



[F3] [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]] supplies an ordered orthonormal basis. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]] gives the vector norm estimates used below.

[F4] Rational numbers are dense in the reals and countable; finite powers of a countable set are countable, and every nonempty countable set is a surjective image of the natural numbers ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]], [[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-finite-powers-of-countable-sets-are-countable]], [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]).



1.1 Choose the ordered orthonormal basis of [F3]. In its coordinates $q(u)=\langle Mu,u\rangle$ is a real continuous quadratic polynomial, bounded on the unit sphere by the finite sum of the absolute matrix entries. By [F4], enumerate all rational-coordinate vectors $y_k\in(\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q)^D$, and put $v_k=y_k/\|y_k\|$ when $y_k\ne0$ and $v_k=e_1$ otherwise. For any unit $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$, coordinatewise rational approximation gives $\|y-x\|<\min(\varepsilon/2,1/2)$ for such a $y$. Then $y\ne0$ and the reverse triangle inequality gives $\|y/\|y\|-x\|\le|1-\|y\||+\|y-x\|\le2\|y-x\|<\varepsilon$. Thus the $v_k$ are dense on the sphere; they are normalizations of rational-coordinate vectors, not necessarily rational-coordinate vectors themselves. Let $m=\sup_{\|u\|=1}q(u)$. For each $n\ge1$ take the least index $k(n)$ with $q(v_{k(n)})>m-1/n$, which exists by continuity and density. This deterministic rule uses no countable choice. By [F1] the bounded sequence $v_{k(n)}$ has a convergent subsequence; its limit has norm one and attains $m$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Let $u$ be a maximizing unit vector and $w\perp u$. Differentiating $q((u+tw)/\|u+tw\|)$ at $t=0$ for real $t$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}\langle Mw,u\rangle=0$. Replacing $w$ by $iw$ shows that the imaginary part also vanishes. Hermiticity gives $\langle Mu,w\rangle=0$ for every $w\perp u$, so $Mu=q(u)u$ with real eigenvalue. Moreover $u^\perp$ is invariant, since $\langle Mw,u\rangle=\langle w,Mu\rangle=0$. Induction on $D$, including the one-dimensional case, gives an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 For $M=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$, define $f(M)=\sum_\lambda f(\lambda)P_\lambda$. The full eigenspaces and their orthogonal projections are intrinsic, so this definition is independent of the basis within each eigenspace. It supplies positive square roots, exponentials and logarithms on positive supports. Finite coordinate sums give $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$, hence invariance under unitary changes of orthonormal basis. Diagonalizing $\rho$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for every complex matrix $A$, and in particular $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho B^*B)=\sum_jp_j\|Bu_j\|^2\ge0$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$, $b=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Y^*Y)$ and $c=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*X)$. Step 3.1 gives $c+za+\overline z\,\overline a+|z|^2b\ge0$ for all complex $z$. If $b>0$, take $z=-\overline a/b$ to get $|a|^2\le bc$. If $b=0$, varying $z$ with arbitrarily large magnitude forces $a=0$, giving the same inequality. This proves the stated weighted Cauchy–Schwarz formula (whose form is conjugate-linear in $X$). [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The density eigenvalues satisfy $p_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)=\sum_jp_j^2\le1$, with equality exactly when one eigenvalue is one and all others vanish. If a rank-one density $\rho=|u\rangle\langle u|$ is $t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $0<t<1$, then every $v\perp u$ has $0=t\langle\sigma v,v\rangle+(1-t)\langle\tau v,v\rangle$. Positivity and the square roots from step 3.1 give $\sigma v=\tau v=0$. Self-adjointness puts their ranges in $\mathbb C u$, and trace one gives $\sigma=\tau=\rho$. Conversely, two positive eigenvalues allow a sufficiently small opposite transfer of weight, yielding distinct densities $\rho_+,\rho_-$ with midpoint $\rho$. Thus precisely the rank-one densities are extreme. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The compact oriented boundaryless Riemannian three-manifold and smooth charged-fluid initial data of [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]], with its sourced Gauss constraint.

[F1] [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]]: $j^a=cNZu^a$, $N>0$, and $g(u,u)=-1$.

[A1] The specified initial electric Gauss equation is $\operatorname{div}_h e=-\mu_0g(j,n)$; it is an explicit hypothesis of this proposition.

[F2] [[def-riemannian-divergence]]: The Riemannian divergence is the scalar determined in each oriented chart by $\mathcal L_e\operatorname{vol}_h=(\operatorname{div}_h e)\operatorname{vol}_h$.

[F3] [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-riemannian-divergence]]: If $h_{ij}$ is the coordinate metric and $e=e^i\partial_i$, then $\operatorname{div}_h e=(\det h)^{-1/2}\partial_i((\det h)^{1/2}e^i)$.

[F4] [[lem-finite-chart-localization-defines-choice-free-integration-and-compact-stokes]]: For a compactly supported smooth $2$-form $\eta$ on an oriented boundaryless smooth three-manifold, its finite chart integral satisfies $\int_\Sigma d\eta=0$.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On an oriented coordinate chart write $\operatorname{vol}_h=\sqrt{\det h}\,dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. Direct contraction gives $\iota_e\operatorname{vol}_h=e^1\sqrt{\det h}\,dx^2\wedge dx^3-e^2\sqrt{\det h}\,dx^1\wedge dx^3+e^3\sqrt{\det h}\,dx^1\wedge dx^2$. Differentiating and reordering the wedge factors gives $d(\iota_e\operatorname{vol}_h)=\partial_i(\sqrt{\det h}\,e^i)dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3=(\operatorname{div}_h e)\operatorname{vol}_h$ by [F3]. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Since $\Sigma$ is compact, $\iota_e\operatorname{vol}_h$ is compactly supported. Apply [F4] to step 1.1 to obtain $\int_\Sigma\operatorname{div}_h e\,\operatorname{vol}_h=0$. Integrating [A1] therefore gives $0=-\mu_0\int_\Sigma g(j,n)\operatorname{vol}_h$, and $\mu_0>0$ implies $\int_\Sigma g(j,n)\operatorname{vol}_h=0$. [step 1.1, A1, F4, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], $j=cNZu$ and hence $-c^{-1}g(j,n)=NZ(-g(u,n))$ pointwise. The definition of $Q_n$ and step 2.1 give $Q_n=0$. No sign assumption on $Z$ is needed. [step 2.1, F1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The data and constraints in the Statement, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, Dependent Choice, and the inspected current CP02 and CP01 draft interfaces below.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[A2] [[def-dependent-choice]]: Assume Dependent Choice.

[F1] [[def-emg-strict-charged-barotropic-system]]: $T_{m,ab}=(\epsilon+p)u_a u_b+pg_{ab}$, $T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}=\mu_0^{-1}(F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\tfrac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd})$, $j=cNZu$, $\nabla^aT_{m,ab}=F_{bc}j^c$, $u(Z)=0$, $dF=0$, and $d\star_gF=\mu_0\iota_j\operatorname{vol}_g$ (equivalently $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$); the stress, current and force sources are algebraic in the state variables.

[F2] [[lem-gr-reduced-einstein-principal-part]]: In harmonic gauge the first-order metric jet $(g,p=\bar\nabla_0g,q_i=\bar\nabla_i g)$ has symmetric principal matrices and positive time matrix $\operatorname{diag}(I,-g^{00}I,(g^{ij}))$ when $g^{00}<0$ and $(g^{ij})>0$; substituting a smooth algebraic stress tensor leaves this block unchanged, and the equations for $p,q_i$ propagate their defining derivative relations.

[F3] [[lem-emg-charged-fluid-positive-symmetric-reduction]]: The strict $(r,u,Z)$ fluid block has symmetric principal matrices and positive time matrix for every future-positive timelike time covector; its Lorentz force and all couplings through the algebraic stress/current are lower order.

[F4] [[lem-emg-charged-fluid-current-conservation]]: The matter balance and transported $Z$ imply $\nabla_a j^a=0$; conditional on the planned CP01 Maxwell-stress identity, $\nabla^a(T_m+T_{\mathrm{EM}})_{ab}=0$ before imposing the Einstein equation.

[F5] [[thm-gr-local-symmetric-hyperbolic-well-posedness]]: Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a periodic quasilinear symmetric-hyperbolic system with smooth coefficient maps on an open state set, compact initial value range in that set, uniformly positive time matrix there, and integer $s\ge5$ has a local solution in $L^\infty H^s\cap C^0H^{s-1}$ with the theorem's classical regularity and uniqueness in that class.

[F6] [[lem-gr-einstein-residual-and-subsidiary-identity]]: On a reduced Einstein solution, $E_{ab}=\tfrac12(\nabla_aH_b+\nabla_bH_a-g_{ab}\nabla_cH^c)$; if $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$, then $\Box_gH_b+\operatorname{Ric}_{ba}H^a=0$.

[F7] [[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]: On a spacelike slice, the Einstein constraints for $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ are exactly $R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}K)^2-|K|^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T(n,n)$ and $\operatorname{div}_hK-D\operatorname{tr}K=\kappa T(n,\cdot)$ under the stated $K$ sign convention.

Reconstruct $F_0$ uniquely from $(e,b)$ by [F12]. For the torus use the global fiber coordinates $y^i=u^i$ on the future unit-velocity hyperboloid; the normalization $g(u,u)=-1$ selects the positive root $u^0=\sqrt{1+h_{ij}u^iu^j}$ on the initial orthogonal slice, so these give a smooth state chart. The CP02 Maxwell block is the current draft interface [L1]: its source-free matrices are symmetric with positive time matrix, and the algebraic current in [F1] changes only its zero-order term. The metric derivative relations propagate by the reduced equations, the velocity coordinates preserve $g(u,u)=-1$ and future orientation, and the enthalpy change is invertible by [F3]. The regularity $h\in H^{s+1}$ and $K,e,b,\epsilon_0,u_0,Z_0\in H^s$ gives the complete first-order initial state in $H^s$. [F1, F2, F3, F11, F12, L1, algebra]

3.1 Put $U=dF$ and $V=d(\star_gF)-\mu_0\iota_j\operatorname{vol}_g$. The sourced Maxwell evolution equations imply $\iota_nU=\iota_nV=0$; hence these are spatial three-forms and uniquely have the form $U=q\,\iota_n\operatorname{vol}_g$, $V=r\,\iota_n\operatorname{vol}_g$. Since $d^2=0$ and [F9] applies, $dU=0$ and $dV=-\mu_0(\nabla_aj^a)\operatorname{vol}_g=0$ by current conservation [F4]. In the torus branch the fields are sufficiently differentiable by step 2.1; the coordinate identity in [F9] therefore applies pointwise at this regularity, and the smooth branch has smooth fields. Expanding $d(q\iota_n\operatorname{vol}_g)$ gives $\nabla_a(qn^a)=0$, or $n(q)+q\nabla_an^a=0$; the identical calculation gives $n(r)+r\nabla_an^a=0$. In a positively oriented normal frame, [F12] and the Hodge component formula [F13] give $F|_\Sigma=\iota_b\operatorname{vol}_h$ and $(*F)|_\Sigma=\iota_e\operatorname{vol}_h$; [F14] then gives $i^*U=(\operatorname{div}_hb)\operatorname{vol}_h$. Also $i^*(\iota_j\operatorname{vol}_g)=-g(j,n)\operatorname{vol}_h$, so [F14] gives $i^*V=(\operatorname{div}_he+\mu_0g(j,n))\operatorname{vol}_h$. Since $n^0=\alpha^{-1}>0$ by the positive-lapse slicing in [L1], the normal flow is transverse to $t=0$; after shrinking, every point lies on a unique normal integral curve from the initial slice by [F10]. Along such a curve, say with parameter $\lambda$, the equations are $q'+(\nabla_an^a)q=0$ and $r'+(\nabla_an^a)r=0$. Multiplying the first by $\exp(\int\nabla_an^a\,d\lambda)$ gives a constant product, so its zero initial value implies $q=0$; the same argument gives $r=0$. Thus $U=V=0$ and both sourced Maxwell equations hold. [step 2.1, F4, F9, F10, F12, F13, F14, L1, given, algebra]

Multiplying the wave equation by $-1$, adjoining $\partial_tW_i-\partial_iV=0$, and multiplying these latter equations by $g^{ji}$ gives a first-order symmetric system with time matrix $A^0=\operatorname{diag}(-g^{00},(g^{ij}))$, cross entries $A^k_{V,W_j}=-g^{kj}$ and $A^k_{W_i,V}=-g^{ik}$, and $VV$ entry $-2g^{0k}$. The Friedrichs commutators $[B^i,J_\delta]\partial_iY$ are bounded in $L^2$ by $C\|\nabla B^i\|_{L^\infty}\|Y\|_{L^2}$ and converge to zero by their kernel formula and density of smooth functions. Thus the integrated inequality passes to the limit. The initial state $Y(0)=0$, so Gronwall forward and with time reversed gives $Y=0$; integrating $V=\partial_tH$ and using $H(0)=0$ gives $H=0$.
